title: Human Nature
full_review:
Writer Charlie Kaufman weaves excess body hair, zany characters, and the notion that sex is at the root of every human motivation into the bizarre romantic comedy "Human Nature" (Fine Line).

Known for the surreal 1999 tale "Being John Malkovich," Kaufman shows sparks of the same originality and eccentric imagination in his new work. He teams up with first-time director Michel Gondry, who previously directed music videos and commercials for Nike and The Gap. But "Human Nature" lacks the energy to keep the strange characters and situations from dragging, eventually turning into a boring mish-mash of scenes. And the characters are strange indeed. Nathan (Tim Robbins) is a behavioral scientist who teaches mice table manners, believing that courtesy and politesse can create a better world. He narrates the story from a drab white room, supposedly heaven or purgatory, where a trickle of blood on his forehead oozes from a bullet wound.

Nathan had always been shy about his sexuality, until he met Lila (Patricia Arquette), a nature writer with a hairy problem. Covered with hair from head to toe, Lila's closest relationship before Nathan was with her electrologist (Rosie Perez). And despite how she feels about him, her hairy body is one secret she keeps hidden from Nathan, painstakingly shaving (back, chest, stomach, face) each night before going to bed.

One day on a nature walk, Lila and Nathan encounter a wild man (Rhys Ifans) living in the woods. Despite Lila's reservations, Nathan takes the man back to his lab where he is installed in a plastic cell and named Puff by Nathan's bombshell French assistant Gabrielle (Miranda Otto). Raised as an ape by his simian-obsessed father, Puff is the perfect project to prove Nathan's theory that a courteous world is a happy world. Nathan schools him not only in polite speech and the correct salad fork, but on the delights of opera, foie gras and smoking jackets.

Regardless of his advice, "When in doubt, don't ever do what you really want to do," the one urge Nathan cannot control in Puff is his sexual drive. A few laughs are procured from this central theme as well as the snappy dialogue and the weird situations in which the characters find themselves. In fact, most of the humor is derived from the tug-of-war between a human's natural desire to be sexual and society's role in controlling it. Yet while it is meant for laughs, some viewers may be put off, realizing, of course, that what makes up a human being is more than just his or her sexuality. And after a few more twists, the premise begins to feel stale and tired. The characters, despite spirited performances by the cast, remain one-dimensional, making it difficult to care even a little about what happens (or happened) to them.

In the end, "Human Nature" is for the birds.

Because of several sexual situations, recurring frontal nudity and intermittent rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
